title: Delhi's AQI Leaps From 65 to 216 in a Day as Calm Weather Traps Pollution
excerpt: Friday's rain briefly gave the capital satisfactory air. With the IMD forecasting dry, still days ahead, the winter pollution season has arrived early — and GRAP Stage 1 is already in force.
body:
• Delhi's AQI swung from 65 to 216 within a day, India Today reported — from satisfactory air straight into the CPCB's 'poor' band (201–300) as rain-washed skies gave way to dry, calm weather.
  • Friday's showers (25.2 mm at the Ridge, 15.9 mm at Safdarjung) had briefly cleaned the air; the IMD expects dry conditions and highs of 31–33°C through October 20, with no rain to disperse pollutants.
  • GRAP Stage 1 anti-pollution measures are in force across Delhi-NCR, the entry level of restrictions that activates when AQI sits in the 'poor' range.
  • For residents: at 'poor' AQI, sensitive groups — children, the elderly, and people with asthma or heart conditions — should limit prolonged outdoor exertion; PM2.5 is the primary pollutant.

Delhi's brief spell of clean air ended in a single day. The capital's Air Quality Index jumped from 65 to 216 — from the 'satisfactory' band deep into 'poor' territory — as the weather pattern that had washed the skies clean gave way to dry, still conditions, India Today reported. The trend is particularly worrying, the report noted, as the capital moves toward winter, when changing weather makes it harder for pollutants to disperse.

Rain cleaned it; calm brought it back

The swing has a clear meteorological explanation. Post-monsoon showers on Friday left measurable rain across the city — 25.2 mm at the Ridge station and 15.9 mm at Safdarjung — temporarily suppressing dust and particulates; the CPCB reading on the evening of October 16 was 96, still 'satisfactory'. But the India Meteorological Department expects mainly dry weather ahead, with daytime highs of 31–33°C through October 20 and no rain in the forecast. Delhi woke on Saturday to haze, light north-westerly winds and PM2.5 as the primary pollutant, according to weather.com's Delhi observations. Light winds are the enemy here: without rain or stronger air movement, traffic, construction dust and regional emissions accumulate near the ground instead of dispersing.

The response machinery is already on

The Commission for Air Quality Management has Stage 1 of the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) in force across Delhi-NCR — the first tier of the capital's pollution playbook, which applies when AQI runs in the 'poor' band of 201–300. Stage 1 focuses on dust control at construction sites, mechanised road sweeping and water sprinkling, action against open waste burning and polluting vehicles, rather than the closures and bans reserved for 'very poor' and 'severe' days. The seasonal pattern is the concern: October is when farm-residue burning in Punjab and Haryana begins, temperatures start falling, and the inversion layer that traps Delhi's winter smog starts to form. An AQI of 216 in mid-October is an early arrival, not the peak.

What it means for families

In the CPCB's health advisory for the 'poor' band, most people face breathing discomfort on prolonged exposure, and people with asthma, heart disease, children and the elderly should reduce prolonged or heavy outdoor exertion. For diaspora families planning Diwali travel to Delhi this week, the practical reading is that conditions can flip within 24 hours — Friday's rain produced a 65 reading, Saturday's calm produced 216 — so checking the morning AQI before outdoor plans, and packing N95 masks for sensitive travellers, is now part of an October trip to the capital.

What to watch

Forecasters see no rain through at least October 20, and temperatures are set to rise slightly by October 21–22. If winds stay light, expect AQI to keep climbing toward the 'very poor' band — the threshold at which GRAP Stage 2 doubles down with parking-fee hikes, more public transport and stricter diesel-generator rules.
